title: How to Photograph Products in Multiple Colors Without Reshooting Each Variant
description: Shooting every color variant is exhausting. Here's the workflow that produces color variations from one shoot.

blocks.text: You have a product in 8 colors. Traditional advice says shoot all 8. Reality: that's 8x the setup, editing, and file management. Most sellers give up and use "swatch" images.
Here's a smarter approach.
The Traditional Approach
Shoot each color variant separately:
Time cost: 8 products × 15 minutes each = 2 hours minimum.
The Smart Approach
Shoot one "hero" product in a neutral color (white, black, or gray). Then use edit-photo.com to:
For actual color-changed product photos, you'll still need to shoot each color for accurate representation. But the presentation work becomes trivial.
When Color-Swap Editing Is Acceptable
For simple products with solid colors (t-shirts, phone cases, mugs), editing the hero product's color can create passable variant images.
Not for:

items.text: Products where color affects the material appearance
Anything customers might return over "color not as pictured"

blocks.text: The Hybrid Strategy
Step 1: Shoot each variant color in a quick session (5 min each with a consistent setup)
Step 2: Edit all through edit-photo.com with identical backgrounds and settings
Step 3: Batch export
Same time as one traditional shoot, but with accurate color representation.
The Variant Swatch Photo
Beyond individual variant photos, create a "swatch" image showing all colors at once:

The Amazon Variant Setup

Amazon parent-child variants show individual color photos when buyers select. If your color-specific photos are inconsistent (different backgrounds, different lighting), buyers subconsciously distrust the listing.
Standardize through edit-photo.com. Every variant photographed and edited identically.

blocks.text: The Time-Math Reality

8 color variants shot separately: 2+ hours
8 color variants shot with hybrid workflow + editing: 45 minutes
Compounding across 20 multi-variant SKUs = weeks saved per year.
